1:
The dating is contested before anything else. Wesley makes the sixth day before the passover the sabbath the Jews called the Great Sabbath; Lightfoot builds the week out from it, putting this supper at the sabbath's going out, when by the custom of the country suppers were more liberal, and the entry into Jerusalem next day. Robertson reasons from the crucifixion instead: if that was a Friday, six days before falls on the preceding sabbath, or more likely the Friday afternoon, since Jesus would have arrived before the sabbath. Henry takes the visit as a preface to the passover, devout men setting time apart beforehand to prepare for a solemnity.

Whose house it was divides them further. Barnes and Clarke follow the earlier Gospels in putting the supper at the house of Simon the leper, Barnes noting that Martha and Lazarus are named precisely because it was not their own house, and that Lazarus at table proves his restoration no illusion. Calvin agrees it was some other house than theirs, since Lazarus is described as one invited along with Christ. Ellicott observes that John alone leaves the place undefined while adding that Martha was still serving and Lazarus present. Robertson sets out the harder problem, that Mark and Matthew place this supper two days before the passover where John puts it immediately on the arrival at Bethany; Bernard, he reports, thinks John here more probably accurate.

On the ointment the comment turns technical. Robertson identifies the pound as the Roman litra of twelve ounces, against the alabaster cruse of the other accounts, and takes the disputed adjective for genuine; Ellicott allows that but thinks it may be a local name. Calvin says it was no simple extract but a compound of many odoriferous substances, and reports from Pliny that ordinary ointment cost ten denarii where the best reached three hundred and ten, so Judas valued it correctly. Gill and Clarke both reckon the three hundred pence in English money. Chrysostom looks past the price: Mary did not take part in the general serving but gave all her attention to the Lord, treating him not as mere man but as God.

Judas is handled with unusual care. Ellicott notes that Matthew ascribes the question to the disciples and Mark to certain persons, while John remembers it was Judas and that the words were characteristic of the man. Calvin thinks the murmuring came from Judas alone and the others were induced to assent, since slander is readily embraced and we are too prone to unfavourable judgments. Barnes explains the bag as a word first used of the case in which musicians kept their pipe-reeds, then of any purse, and Lightfoot traces it through the Talmudists to a coffer for laying up money. Clarke presses the verb further than the others, arguing from its use elsewhere that Judas did not merely carry what was put in but stole it.

The answer is read as a defence of one act and not a rule. Calvin insists on the distinction between Mary's extraordinary action and the daily service due to Christ, and calls those apes rather than imitators who serve him by costly display. Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson agree that the better manuscripts read not that she has kept the ointment but that she may keep it for the day of the embalming, which Ellicott connects with a burial lately performed in that place, in the person of a man now at the table. Augustine takes the last clause of bodily presence only, since in majesty and invisible grace the promise holds that he is with us to the end of the world, and finds in Judas a figure of the wicked within the Church. Chrysostom broadens it to power as well as wealth, the one breeding covetousness and the other pride, and notes that here the multitude believes where the rulers do not.
9:
How the news travelled is easily accounted for. Gill points out that Bethany lay only two miles from Jerusalem, so the report soon reached the city; Ellicott supposes pilgrims from Jericho carried it, to people who had already come up from the country and were asking after him. Clarke notes in passing a habit of this Gospel, that John, being a Galilean, often gives the name of Jews to the inhabitants of Jerusalem. Robertson stops at the phrase for the crowd, where the article stands oddly placed, and reports Westcott's suggestion that the two words had come to be treated as a single compound noun. Ellicott adds what the verse itself adds, that many came not only for Jesus but to see Lazarus; and Calvin reads the whole celebrity as providential, since the nearer the death approached, the more necessary it was that the name of Christ should be widely known, and God intended so remarkable a proof of his divinity to have many witnesses.

The plot against Lazarus draws the sharpest language in the chapter. Barnes states the principle flatly, that when men are determined not to believe there is no end to the crimes they are driven to: the evidence was irresistible, they could neither deny it nor prevent its effect, and so the witness had to be removed before the death of Jesus could be managed quietly. Lazarus was innocent and no charge could be brought against him, which is his point exactly, that unbelief stops at no crime. Clarke puts the same thing as an absurdity: how blind not to see that he who had raised the man after four days could raise him again though they killed him a thousand times. Calvin calls it worse than insane fury, and traces it not to mistake or folly but to the spirit of giddiness with which Satan torments the wicked, so that they did not shrink from making war on God.

Two of the witnesses look at who was doing it. Ellicott observes that the chief priests were for the most part Sadducees, so that the living Lazarus contradicted their own doctrine that there is no resurrection as well as bearing witness to the man they had condemned; he adds that the word does not mean they reached a final decision, only that they took counsel and watched their opportunity. Robertson agrees the Sadducees were now especially active, and guesses at their reasoning, that if they killed both Jesus and Lazarus then Lazarus at least would stay dead.

The effect is measured in the tenses. Ellicott renders the last verse were going away and were believing, two words marking two acts, a withdrawal from the authority of the priests and a faith in Jesus, both still continuing. Robertson calls the first an inchoative imperfect, that they began to withdraw, and judges there was now danger of a mass movement of the people. Gill keeps the reason in view, that the man himself was the living and abiding witness of the miracle. Wesley draws the one inference nobody else makes, that here is the plain reason why the earlier evangelists, writing while Lazarus was still alive, did not tell his story at all.
12:
The crowd is identified before it is described. Robertson dates the day to Palm Sunday and takes the phrase for the common people rather than a great multitude; Wesley says they were chiefly Galileans and not men of Jerusalem, and Henry makes the point with an edge, that these were country people from remote parts, the nearer the temple the further from the Lord of the temple. Gill calls it a crowded passover, every male being obliged to appear and multitudes of women coming besides; Lightfoot supplies a rabbinic estimate of the throng, King Agrippa counting the paschal lambs by having one kidney of each laid aside and reaching six hundred thousand pair. Ellicott observes that John alone gives this note of time, tying the entry to the stay at Bethany where the others describe the approach from Jericho.

The palms are read as a deliberate sign. Ellicott renders the phrase literally as the palm branches of the palm trees, and notes that neither word occurs elsewhere in the New Testament; Robertson adds that to carry palms was a mark of triumphant homage to a victor or a king, and points to Simon's entry into Jerusalem in Maccabees for the same usage. Calvin treats the branches as an emblem of victory and peace and the shout as a confession, since the psalm they quote was composed with reference to the Messiah, so in using it they acknowledged Jesus as the one promised to the fathers.

On the ass the comment is partly chronological and partly harmonising. Chrysostom draws the calendar out of the law: the lamb was shut up on the tenth day and killed on the fourteenth, and so the spotless Lamb went up to Jerusalem five days before his immolation. Calvin resolves the apparent contradiction between the Gospels by taking Matthew's account as a synecdoche, and Robertson agrees that rightly understood Matthew has Jesus riding the colt only. Robertson adds the force of the prophecy, that the ass was ridden in peace as the horse in war, so Zechariah pictures one coming peaceably; Wesley finds the same in the opening words, that the meekness of his coming forbids fear.

What the disciples did not see at the time is treated as a mark of the writer. Ellicott calls it a touch exactly in John's manner, remembering the difference in receptivity before and after Pentecost, and how the old Scriptures took on new life as the Spirit brought their words to mind. Calvin gives the figure: the seed does not spring as soon as it is sown, and the shout was to the apostles an unmeaning exhibition until the Lord opened their eyes after the resurrection, though they were his servants in fulfilling the prophecy. Clarke makes the general rule, that only in the light of the new covenant is the old fully understood, and Wesley the practical one, that the design of God's dispensations is seldom understood at first, so the great work of faith is to embrace what we shall know hereafter.

Two crowds meet, and the chapter says so twice. Ellicott distinguishes the people who had been at the grave and bore witness from the multitude that came out because they had heard, and Robertson makes the same division, one crowd following and one going to meet him; Barnes and Clarke take the Pharisees' despairing word about the world as an idiom for the bulk of the people, Clarke comparing the French phrase for everybody, Lightfoot noting that the Talmudists speak the same way. Robertson calls the saying a pathetic confession of failure, the plotters blaming one another for a bungled plot. Calvin hears something more dangerous, men reproaching their own slothfulness to work themselves up to extremity, and draws the lesson that if the enemies of God persevere so obstinately in evil, we ought to be far steadier in a just undertaking.
20:
Who the Greeks were is the first question. Barnes and Clarke set out three opinions, that they were Greek-speaking Jews of the dispersion, proselytes of the gate, or mere Gentiles drawn by the temple's fame; Ellicott and Robertson settle on the middle answer, insisting the word means Hellenes and not Hellenists, and taking them for God-fearers admitted to Judaism's privileges. Bede supplies the setting, the temple being famous enough to draw Gentiles from distant countries, the eunuch of Candace among them. Lightfoot narrows the guess to Syro-Grecians of Decapolis or Gadara, who bordered on Galilee and would be readier to seek Jesus out. Calvin dissents from the Gentile reading on legal grounds, since Roman law punished a man who left his native worship for the Jewish. Wesley cares only what they signify, a prelude of the Gentile Church. Henry dates the visit a day or two after the entry, that day having been taken up with public work.

The approach through two apostles is noticed as a coincidence. Ellicott finds it striking that they came to the only two apostles bearing Greek names, fellow-townsmen and friends who may themselves have had some connection with Greek life. Robertson calls Andrew a man of wisdom for a crisis and names the difficulty, the middle wall of partition that would puzzle Peter at Joppa. Calvin reads the indirect approach as reverence, which always begets modesty.

The answer is not an answer, and they say so. Ellicott calls the words the utterance of his own thoughts rather than a reply, though he thinks the Greeks heard them. Robertson identifies the hour as the predestined one, spoken of from the beginning as not yet come, and says the request from the Greeks stirred the heart of Jesus to its depths. Calvin takes the glorifying not of the death, as most do, but of the publication of the gospel, so the disciples should not lose courage when the doctrine was to be proclaimed through the world. Wesley adds the one qualification, that he must suffer first.

The grain of wheat is where the comment gathers. Lightfoot paraphrases the logic that makes it an answer: the Gentiles desire to see me, and the time draws on when I must be glorified in their conversion, but the corn brings forth nothing unless first thrown into the ground to die. Calvin presses the paradox, that sowing appears to destroy the seed and is the cause of far more abundant increase. Ellicott calls the analogy not a mere comparison but an instance of one law of life given to the moral and physical worlds alike; Robertson denies any borrowing from the Eleusinian mysteries, noting that Paul uses the same figure of the resurrection. Wesley observes that out of thousands of seeds our Lord singles out almost the only one which dies in the earth, matched only by millet and the large bean.

The hard saying that follows is read as the same law applied to the hearer. Ellicott prefers the present tense, the man who loves his life losing it already in the moment of seeking to save it, and keeps the Greeks in view as volunteer disciples learning what discipleship was. Calvin defines the terms: the man who cannot leave the world except by constraint loves his life, and he who advances courageously to death hates it, though life is not to be hated absolutely, being among the highest of God's blessings. Chrysostom says the present life is sweet only to those riveted to it, since a man who looks at the beauty of heaven despises it as a lesser beauty when a greater appears. Barnes and Clarke take the next verse of persecution, Clarke expecting the disciple who lays down his life to receive it with everlasting honour. Gill keeps it plain, that a man so in love with this life as to deny the faith loses both.
27:
The troubled soul is taken as proof of a real humanity. Chrysostom supplies the objection it answers, that the disciples might have said it was easy for one beyond the reach of pain to talk philosophically about death; so he lets them see that he is himself in an agony and yet will not decline it merely to relieve himself. Clarke says he took our weaknesses that he might sanctify them, and that nature abhors death by God's own implanting. Robertson observes that John, proving the deity throughout, everywhere assumes the humanity, and gives no Gethsemane because this stands in its place. Calvin admits the passage seems to contradict the courage just urged on the disciples, and answers that it is in perfect harmony, as every believer knows by experience.

The broken question that follows is read as inarticulacy, not indecision. Barnes hears intense anxiety, as if it were under debate whether the work of redemption should be abandoned. Wesley denies it means what shall I choose, since the heart was fixed on the Father's will; he laboured rather for utterance, and the two clauses following seem to have glanced through his mind in one moment, which human language cannot so express. Henry marks the strangeness of the word, coming in the middle of pleasing prospects where one would expect him to say his soul was pleased.

The prayer is short and the witnesses weigh its emphasis. Ellicott makes the pronoun emphatic and compares the Lord's Prayer, the Son's glory lying in the glorifying of the Father's name. Robertson calls it the prayer of the spirit against the flesh of the verse before. Clarke takes the name for God himself in all his attributes, more abundantly glorified by this death than ever before. Wesley parses the answer from heaven into halves, glorified by the entrance into this hour and to be glorified by the passing through.

The voice divides the crowd, and Ellicott makes that division his argument for an eyewitness: the preservation of what the people thought at the time could hardly be a later hand's insertion, and runs against everything such a writer would want. Barnes explains the two reports, some taking it for a natural phenomenon, others recalling the Jewish opinion that God speaks to men only through angels. Clarke reports Bishop Pearce's guess that there was thunder as well as a voice, so those at a distance heard only the one, and Wetstein's that it came in the language then in use, unintelligible to Greeks. Wesley draws the lesson that in the most glorious revelations something may remain obscure to exercise faith, while Calvin calls it monstrous that so evident a miracle left the assembly unmoved, and says the same happens daily, many being as little affected by the Gospel as if it came from a mortal man.

The three sayings at the end are read as one victory. Robertson notes there is no article, so it is a judgement and not the judgement, the next few days being the test of this world; Satan had claimed the world in the temptation, and Jesus, not denying his power then, here proclaims the final victory. Lightfoot shows the phrase was common among the Jewish writers, who meant the angel into whose hands the world was delivered. Calvin hears in the word not condemnation but the restoring of a well-ordered state, the Hebrew term so translated meaning good order. Clarke takes the judgement of the punishment about to fall on the Jewish nation, and the casting out as the overthrow of Satan's kingdom by the calling of the Gentiles. On the lifting up Gill hears the brazen serpent and reads a violent, public death; Ellicott makes the pronoun strongly emphatic, the conqueror set against the vanquished. Calvin turns it into an image: the cross is a chariot by which he raises men with himself to the Father.
34:
The objection is a scriptural one, and the witnesses take some care with it. Augustine notes that the crowd understood him to be speaking of his own death, and that though he had not used the title in the sentence they challenge, they remembered how often he used it of himself. Lightfoot explains the appeal as a formula, out of the law being set against out of the scribes. Ellicott agrees the term covers the whole Old Testament and finds in the objection a specimen of rabbinic theology, reading the promises of an abiding kingdom as a temporal reign; Barnes traces the same opinion to the interpreters, and points to the passages promising a priest for ever and an everlasting dominion.

The answers to it divide. Clarke denies the premise outright, that no part of Scripture ever said the Messiah should not die, while several say expressly that he must die, and for the sin of the world. Calvin grants both halves and blames the selection: it was plainly said that Christ would die and that his kingdom would afterwards flourish to the end of the world, but they seize the second clause alone, and malice blinds them in the clearest light. Wesley reconciles the two in a line, that he first dies and then abides for ever. Chrysostom treats the question as bad faith rather than error, since deceit is weak and easily detected however it be daubed with ten thousand colours, like whitewash on a decayed wall. Henry puts the failure more gently, that they drew false notions from Scripture by overlooking the prophecies of his suffering; Gill calls them cavillers. Lightfoot turns their text against the rabbis, who fixed the length of Messiah's days at forty years, or seventy, or three generations, expecting eternity only afterwards.

That the reply is indirect is noticed by nearly everyone. Ellicott prefers to render the connecting word therefore rather than then, since their question prompted it, and observes that the narrative does not say he answered them, what follows being no direct answer. Barnes reads the indirection as tact, since Jesus saw they were offended by the mention of his death and worked round to the same point another way, never rousing men's prejudices needlessly nor shrinking from unpalatable truth. Robertson says plainly that he would not argue theology with a crowd who could not follow it, and fell back on the figure he had used of himself before. Calvin hears both admonition and sharp reproof: they are charged with shutting their eyes against the light, and threatened that it will shortly be taken away.

What the light means is settled the same way by three of them. Calvin insists it is not the bodily presence but the Gospel, so the departure threatened is the removal of preaching rather than of a person; Wesley makes it I and my doctrine; Clarke keeps the figure moving, a light about to disappear for a short time and afterwards to shine with greater lustre, though not to the comfort of those who reject its beams.

The closing exhortation turns on becoming rather than being. Ellicott would render it according as ye have the light, and takes becoming sons of light for the familiar thought of this Gospel, that the believer grows like the one he believes in. Robertson identifies it as a Hebrew idiom amounting to enlightened men, and recalls that Jesus called his disciples the light of the world. Clarke presses the sonship hard: as truly as a child is the produce of his own parent and partakes of his nature, so they were to have nothing in them but truth and righteousness. On the hiding at the end Clarke will not have a miracle where a withdrawal suffices, and Calvin explains that he withdrew from the adversaries, not from the disciples who had followed him to the temple.
37:
The unbelief is stated as a summary, and they say so. Barnes reads the verse not of miracles wrought that day but of all the works done in the nation's sight, John giving the result of the ministry; Ellicott infers that the signs of the earlier Gospels were well known to John's readers. Robertson notes there is no yet in the Greek and makes the imperfect stubborn: they kept on not believing in the face of the light. Clarke puts the fault in the will, blinded by their passions and hardened against the truth. Calvin gives the pastoral reason: no one should be perplexed at Christ being despised, since the testimony given him was clear and undoubted, and the failure lay in eyes that would not behold the glory openly displayed.

The prophecy that follows raises the hard question at once. Chrysostom asks why Christ came at all if he knew they would not believe, and answers that the prophets had foretold this very unbelief, so his coming made it manifest to their confusion. Clarke would render the connecting word thus rather than that, since it names no one's purpose. Barnes agrees they did not reject him so that a prophecy might be fulfilled, but that by rejecting him the same thing happened as in Isaiah's day. Calvin denies that the prediction laid any necessity on the Jews, since the thing must have happened had the prophet never spoken; it sets before our eyes, as in a mirror, what would otherwise have seemed incredible.

The harder verse, that they could not believe, is handled carefully. Barnes takes the word could as the Bible often uses it, of an obstacle that makes a result certain. Robertson insists John is not absolving them of moral responsibility, only showing the words had to be fulfilled. Calvin grants the saying is harsh and answers that the foreknowledge of God is not itself the cause of events, while Clarke and Wesley make the blinding judicial, God giving them up to the hardness they had chosen by rejecting prophets and miracles together.

On the blinding itself the witnesses guard the text. Gill says it matters little whether the subject is God or Christ or the wickedness itself, since God blinds by no positive act but by leaving men to their hardness and denying the grace that alone could cure it. Barnes reads the prophet's commission the same way, a message whose effect, given the hardness of the hearers, would be to blind them. Clarke refuses outright the reading that God was unwilling they should turn lest he heal them, and refers the words to national judgment. Ellicott observes that the passage is quoted three times in the New Testament, by our Lord of his own teaching, by John of its rejection and by Paul of the Jews at Rome, yet all who quote it are themselves witnesses that within Israel there were eyes that did see.

The closing verses turn on glory of two kinds. Lightfoot and Barnes note the Targum's habit of writing the glory of God where the Hebrew has God, no man being able to see him; Clarke and Wesley draw the conclusion John intends, that the glory Isaiah saw was Jehovah's and John calls it the glory of Jesus. Robertson adds that Isaiah saw it with spiritual vision, as Abraham saw his day; Calvin, that the prophet accommodated his teaching to a reign still future. Of the rulers who believed and would not say so, Henry marks the struggle between conviction and corruption; Calvin calls their faith a striking instance of grace amidst a general madness, insisting that what held them back was ambition, not scruple. Chrysostom names the passion: vainglory, like the love of money, is a root and mother of other mischiefs, and these men were broken off from the faith by love of honour.
44:
The cry is placed carefully. Ellicott argues that the word forbids taking these verses of any private word to the disciples, since it implies public teaching, so some preaching followed the withdrawal a few verses earlier; Clarke reads it as the resumption of the discourse broken off there. Robertson treats it as a summary of what was already said, and observes that John closes the public ministry here without the Synoptic last day in the temple. Henry calls it the farewell sermon to the Jews and the last public discourse, Wesley the epilogue and recapitulation of them all. Gill hears in the loud voice the vehemence of his spirit and a purpose, that the hearers be left inexcusable.

The first saying is guarded by all of them in the same way. Barnes, Clarke and Wesley all supply the missing word: faith does not terminate on Christ alone but passes through him to the one who sent him. Chrysostom makes it an answer to the fear that had silenced the rulers: why are you afraid to believe in me, when your faith through me passes to God? Calvin hears the same encouragement with a reproof folded into it, and takes the point to be that faith relies on no mortal man but on God. On the verse following, Barnes presses the other way: this is a strong confirmation of equality with God, since of no man could it be said that to see him was to see God, and to say it of Paul or Isaiah would have been blasphemy. Gill cautions that this is not seeing with bodily eyes, since many saw Christ who never saw the Father and were offended at the meanness of his appearance.

The light is taken up from the earlier part of the chapter. Clarke says that before this coming all was darkness, that at his rising the darkness is dispersed, but that it profits only those whose eyes are open to receive the rays. Robertson puts it in four words, that light dispels darkness.

A textual point governs the next verse. Ellicott, Clarke and Robertson agree the better reading is not believe them not but keep them not, Clarke setting the sequence out as a ladder: a man must hear in order to believe, believe in order to keep, keep in order to be saved. Barnes reads the disclaimer of judging as a matter of timing, not principle: it was not the present purpose to condemn, so no sentence is passed while opportunity remains. Calvin says the same in his own key: Christ begins here to strike the rebellious but mitigates the severity, delaying sentence because he has come for the salvation of all.

The judgment deferred is then lodged in the word itself. Barnes observes that Christ needs no voice of his own to condemn such a man, since conscience and the remembered words will do it; Clarke makes the doctrine the standard of trial at the last; Robertson says the very word rejected will confront the rejecter; Ellicott notes that the verb for rejecting means rather to nullify and occurs nowhere else in this Gospel. Calvin calls it a dreadful threatening, comparing the saying that the Jews would need no other accuser than the Moses in whom they boasted. Clarke takes the disclaimer that follows as a minister's as well as a Son's, that he had not spoken for secular interest nor set himself up to be maintained by disciples; Robertson marks the perfect tense a permanent commission. On the last verse Gill denies that the commandment meant is the law, which promised only the continuance of natural life; Barnes finds in it the reason for the earnestness of the whole ministry, that eternal life hung on the faithful delivery of the message; Wesley closes simply, that the commandment kept is both the way to everlasting life and the beginning of it.
